title: Why Building an Eval Platform Is Harder Than It Looks — Braintrust
talk_summary: A Braintrust solutions engineer explains why eval platforms are systems problems, not spreadsheets: you need to capture production traces, turn failure modes into offline test cases, iterate, and re-ship in a continuous improvement loop. The talk is mostly conceptual and vendor-framed, but the trace-to-eval flywheel and the 'coding agent runs the evals' pattern are directly copyable.

takeaways.what_they_do: Log every input, output, and step of live agent runs, define success/failure dimensions, then harvest real failure scenarios into offline test cases so fixes don't introduce regressions.
Instead of humans driving evals, they point a coding agent at the trace store and codebase and let it find bad traces, run evals, and log results; humans only review outcomes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: tell your coding agent of choice, 'Find me all traces in the last 24 hours where the user had a poor experience. Run the evals for me.'

takeaways.technique: Treat traces as large semi-structured payloads
takeaways.what_they_do: Warns that agent traces are deeply nested semi-structured JSON, sometimes hundreds of MB per interaction, and that naive warehouses collapse; they built a query abstraction (BTQL) for real-time plus long-running reads.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agent traces are nasty. They are semi-structured JSON... hundreds of megabytes... your typical cloud data warehouses kind of collapse

takeaways.what_they_do: Evolve from logging to letting non-technical users tweak system prompt, model, and parameters and compare outputs side-by-side on the same curated test inputs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I want to be able to tweak a system prompt. I want to change the underlying model. I want to iterate on some parameter values.

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues quality requires pre-defined dimensions of success and failure so scores are comparable over time rather than ad hoc human judgment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You create the dimensions of failure and success because you know the outcomes.
